question.text: What does the option Greek 'theta' measure, and what is its broad implication for option holders over time?

answer.text: Theta measures the change in option premium for a change in time to expiry; options tend to lose time value each day throughout their life
Theta measures the change in option premium for a change in the underlying price
Theta measures the change in option premium for a change in volatility
Theta indicates that time value only changes on the expiry day itself

explanation.text: The Logic: Theta is the option Greek that captures the sensitivity of the option premium to the passage of time. As time to expiry shortens, the time-value component of the premium tends to erode, so options generally lose time value each day, all else equal — which is what "time decay" refers to. The Trap: The sensitivity of the option premium to a change in the underlying price is delta, not theta. The sensitivity to a change in volatility is vega. And time decay is not a single expiry-day event — it accrues over the option's life. Note: The NISM Series IV (Interest Rate Derivatives) workbook page reviewed defines theta as a one-day measure of time decay and says options tend to lose time value each day. The earlier framing involving square-root-of-time acceleration and final-week vs first-month comparisons was not located in the workbook pages reviewed, so this item is reframed to the source-supported core definition.
